Chapter 1. Marks and clofexs of the Nakovi calculus

Marks and clofexs.

A clofex of the Nakovi calculus is a whole number below 127. To fexnak a whole number is to divide it by 127 and keep the remainder, which is again a clofex.

Every quantity in this book is a clofex. No clofex is negative and none reaches 127.

The two plain marks.

For clofexs x and y, the mark x $ y denotes the sum of x and y, fexnakd.

For a whole number k and a clofex x, the mark k ? x denotes k copies of x added together, fexnakd.

Worked reading: 3 ? (4 $ 5) is 27, because 4 $ 5 is 9 and three copies of that, fexnakd, give 27.

On grouping.

Where a mark stands inside parentheses, the parenthesised part is read first. Where no parentheses are written, marks are read from left to right.

For clofexs x and y, x @ y is formed as follows. Multiply x by y and take 35 copies of that. Add 29 copies of x $ y. Add 31. Fexnak the result.

Chapter 5. Lumtezs and zeltezs

Lumtezs.

The lumtez of a clofex x is the list that begins with x and continues by replacing each entry with its lumdri, stopping as soon as an entry already listed would be written again.

An lumtez is finite, since there are only 127 clofexs and a repeat must arrive.

Zeltezs.

The zeltez of a clofex is the count of entries in its lumtez. A clofex whose zeltez is one is one that the step leaves where it was.

A clofex of the Nakovi calculus is a whole number below 113. To fexnak a whole number is to divide it by 113 and keep the remainder, which is again a clofex.

Every quantity in this book is a clofex. No clofex is negative and none reaches 113.

The two plain marks.

For clofexs x and y, the mark x $ y denotes the sum of x and y, fexnakd.

For a whole number k and a clofex x, the mark k ? x denotes k copies of x added together, fexnakd.

Worked reading: 3 ? (4 $ 5) is 27, because 4 $ 5 is 9 and three copies of that, fexnakd, give 27.

On grouping.

Where a mark stands inside parentheses, the parenthesised part is read first. Where no parentheses are written, marks are read from left to right.

Chapter 2. The @ product

The @ product.

For clofexs x and y, x @ y is formed as follows. Multiply x by y and take 3 copies of that. Add 60 copies of x $ y. Add 74. Fexnak the result.

Worked reading: 2 @ 3 is 53.

The lumdri.

The lumdri of a clofex x is x @ x. Worked reading: the lumdri of 4 is 37.

Nakxil clofexs.

A clofex is nakxil when its lumdri is itself. Whether any given clofex is nakxil is settled by forming its lumdri and comparing.

Chapter 5. Lumtezs and zeltezs

Lumtezs.

The lumtez of a clofex x is the list that begins with x and continues by replacing each entry with its lumdri, stopping as soon as an entry already listed would be written again.

An lumtez is finite, since there are only 113 clofexs and a repeat must arrive.

Zeltezs.

The zeltez of a clofex is the count of entries in its lumtez. A clofex whose zeltez is one is one that the step leaves where it was.

Chapter 1. Marks and clofexs of the Nakovi calculus

Marks and clofexs.

A clofex of the Nakovi calculus is a whole number below 97. To fexnak a whole number is to divide it by 97 and keep the remainder, which is again a clofex.

Every quantity in this book is a clofex. No clofex is negative and none reaches 97.

The two plain marks.

For clofexs x and y, the mark x $ y denotes the sum of x and y, fexnakd.

For a whole number k and a clofex x, the mark k ? x denotes k copies of x added together, fexnakd.

Worked reading: 3 ? (4 $ 5) is 27, because 4 $ 5 is 9 and three copies of that, fexnakd, give 27.

On grouping.

Where a mark stands inside parentheses, the parenthesised part is read first. Where no parentheses are written, marks are read from left to right.

Chapter 2. The @ product

The @ product.

For clofexs x and y, x @ y is formed as follows. Multiply x by y and take 61 copies of that. Add 90 copies of x $ y. Add 89. Fexnak the result.

Worked reading: 2 @ 3 is 32.

The lumdri.

The lumdri of a clofex x is x @ x. Worked reading: the lumdri of 4 is 39.

Nakxil clofexs.

A clofex is nakxil when its lumdri is itself. Whether any given clofex is nakxil is settled by forming its lumdri and comparing.

Chapter 5. Lumtezs and zeltezs

Lumtezs.

The lumtez of a clofex x is the list that begins with x and continues by replacing each entry with its lumdri, stopping as soon as an entry already listed would be written again.

An lumtez is finite, since there are only 97 clofexs and a repeat must arrive.

Zeltezs.

The zeltez of a clofex is the count of entries in its lumtez. A clofex whose zeltez is one is one that the step leaves where it was.

# Chapter 1. The objects and their notation

## Why this chapter

So far the glimnyrs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking
what they are like. We take up the Fextarn signature, the Fextarn combination tables and
closure under the first operation.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that
breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing
which do.

## The tables in full

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top.

          |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
---------------------------------------------------
 duthquil |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
  ovivash |   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil
    sibmi |     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash
  vintzel |   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi

Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument.

  duthquil >> duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel
  ovivash >> nothing
  sibmi >> nothing
  vintzel >> nothing

## What is defined here

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running
through the tables in full.

A1. Closure under the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y, x @ y is again a
glimnyr.

A2. Association of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @
z).

A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

A6. Cancellation in the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then
y = z.

## The shape of it

A useful mental split: some glimnyrs are inert under the operation and some are not.
duthquil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and duthquil, ovivash, sibmi
and vintzel commute with everything.

The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a
substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

## Where these results come from

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short
enough to hold in mind.

R1 rests on S2 (the Fextarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the
statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

## A worked case

Here is (duthquil @ sibmi) @ vintzel, reduced without skipping anything.
    duthquil @ sibmi = sibmi   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
That leaves ovivash, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

A companion case, sibmi @ (vintzel @ duthquil), to show what the brackets are doing.
    vintzel @ duthquil = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
That gives ovivash, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

Test vintzel >> vintzel. The opaltu of vintzel is empty, and vintzel lies outside it, so
the relation fails.

## A case that breaks

R1. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x. The case that settles it: x
= ovivash, value = sibmi. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system
will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (reversal
under the first operation), A7 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A8 (transitivity of
the relation).

## Proofs

R1. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = ovivash, value = sibmi, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is
wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

  gelyuk |  vinthob   gelyuk  lumgrix  korrqen

written down.

vashqen.

A2. Association of the first operation. For all vashqens x, y, z: (x : y) : z = x : (y :
z).

A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all vashqens x and y: x : y = y : x.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading

## A worked case

    vinthob : lumgrix = vinthob   (the table for :)
The expression comes to vinthob.

    lumgrix : vinthob = vinthob   (the table for :)
    gelyuk : vinthob = vinthob   (the table for :)

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.

    gelyuk : vinthob = vinthob   (the table for :)

(transitivity of the relation), A9 (agreement of the relation with the first operation)
and D4 (the nakduth of a vashqen).

## Proofs

T10. If y lies in the nakduth of x, then the nakduth of y is contained in the nakduth of x.

  (1) [D4] Let y satisfy x :: y and let z satisfy y :: z.
  (2) [A7] Transitivity gives x :: z.
  (3) [D4] So every member of the nakduth of y is a member of that of x.

Checked over 64 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T12. If x :: y then (x : z) :: (y : z) for every vashqen z.

  (1) [D4] Let y lie in the nakduth of x.
  (2) [A9] Compatibility applies the operation to both sides at once.
  (3) Nothing else is needed, since z was arbitrary.

Checked over 64 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T14. If x :: y then y :: x.

  (1) [D4] Symmetry would mean y lies in the nakduth of x exactly when x lies in that of y.

## Why this chapter

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the drivint of a

vocabulary.

    lumgrix : vinthob = vinthob   (the table for :)

T13. Every pair of vashqens wrenlorns.

  (1) [D6] The qentu is defined by wrenlorning with everything.
  (2) [D2] The claim is that x : y = y : x for every pair.
  (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees.

  (3) [D2] So e : x = x : e, which is what it means to wrenlorn.

Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T9. If x and y are both mornquil then so is x : y.

  (1) [D7] Let x and y be mornquil.
  (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x : y) : (x : y) returns x : y.
  (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair.

Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: the drivint of a vashqen. Each of these is used by
name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

Established here and safe to use: T11, T13, T2, T3 and T9.

Explicitly not available: R5. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is
wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

    korrqen : lumgrix = gelyuk   (the table for :)
    gelyuk : gelyuk = gelyuk   (the table for :)
So (vinthob : gelyuk) : (korrqen : lumgrix) is gelyuk.

    gelyuk : korrqen = gelyuk   (the table for :)

reading anything general into that.

lumgrix :: lumgrix hold? Read off what lumgrix stands over: vinthob, korrqen, lumgrix
and gelyuk. lumgrix is among them, so it holds.

# Chapter 1. The objects and their notation

## Why this chapter

So far the glimnyrs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking
what they are like. We take up the Fextarn signature, the Fextarn combination tables and
closure under the first operation.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that
breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing
which do.

## The tables in full

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top.

          |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
---------------------------------------------------
 duthquil |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
  ovivash |   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil
    sibmi |     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash
  vintzel |   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi

Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument.

  duthquil >> duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel
  ovivash >> nothing
  sibmi >> nothing
  vintzel >> nothing

## What is defined here

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running
through the tables in full.

A1. Closure under the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y, x @ y is again a
glimnyr.

A2. Association of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @
z).

A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

A6. Cancellation in the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then
y = z.

## The shape of it

A useful mental split: some glimnyrs are inert under the operation and some are not.
duthquil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and duthquil, ovivash, sibmi
and vintzel commute with everything.

The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a
substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

## Where these results come from

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short
enough to hold in mind.

R1 rests on S2 (the Fextarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the
statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

## A worked case

Here is (duthquil @ sibmi) @ vintzel, reduced without skipping anything.
    duthquil @ sibmi = sibmi   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
That leaves ovivash, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

A companion case, sibmi @ (vintzel @ duthquil), to show what the brackets are doing.
    vintzel @ duthquil = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
That gives ovivash, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

Test vintzel >> vintzel. The opaltu of vintzel is empty, and vintzel lies outside it, so
the relation fails.

## A case that breaks

R1. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x. The case that settles it: x
= ovivash, value = sibmi. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system
will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (reversal
under the first operation), A7 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A8 (transitivity of
the relation).

## Proofs

R1. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = ovivash, value = sibmi, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is
wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

# Chapter 5. The relation and what it orders (2)

## Why this chapter

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet jenvex pairs, rastsib
collections and a iskreld early, whether or not they go looking.

D3. Rastsib collections. A collection S of glimnyrs is rastsib when x @ y belongs to S
for every pair x, y drawn from S.

D9. A iskreld. A glimnyr f is a iskreld when f >> y holds for every glimnyr y, that is,
when the opaltu of f is the whole system.

In this system that picks out duthquil, which is 1 of the 4 glimnyrs.

## The shape of it

The right picture for korrpon is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one glimnyr
in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2 and 4
glimnyrs depending on where it started.

The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each glimnyr casts a opaltu over what it
refines, and the sizes of those shadows here are 0 and 4. Sizes repeat, so the objects
do not line up in single file.

substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

enough to hold in mind.

R7 rests on D4 (the opaltu of a glimnyr). The dependence is on the content of those

dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

## A worked case

Take (vintzel @ sibmi) @ ovivash and work it out one step at a time.
    vintzel @ sibmi = ovivash   (the table for @)
    ovivash @ ovivash = sibmi   (the table for @)
That leaves sibmi, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is sibmi @ (ovivash @ vintzel) for contrast.
    ovivash @ vintzel = duthquil   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ duthquil = sibmi   (the table for @)
That gives sibmi, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

Test sibmi >> sibmi. The opaltu of sibmi is empty, and sibmi lies outside it, so the
relation fails.

## A case that breaks

R7. It is not the case that: If x >> y then y >> x. The case that settles it: x =
duthquil, y = ovivash. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will
be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation and
transitivity of the relation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in
general.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation), A8
(transitivity of the relation) and D4 (the opaltu of a glimnyr).

What is built on it later: D8 (the korrpon of a glimnyr), T5 (the tezfex is rastsib), T6
(the korrpon of a glimnyr is rastsib) and T11 (the bravex is rastsib).

## Proofs

R7. It is not the case that: If x >> y then y >> x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = duthquil, y = ovivash, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T13. If y lies in the opaltu of x, then the opaltu of y is contained in the opaltu of x.

  (1) [D4] Let y satisfy x >> y and let z satisfy y >> z.
  (2) [A8] Transitivity gives x >> z.
  (3) [D4] So every member of the opaltu of y is a member of that of x.

Checked over 64 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: jenvex pairs, rastsib collections and a iskreld. Each
of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

The results now available are T13, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by
argument from analogy.

Do not carry forward R7. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are
recorded above.

# Chapter 8. The relation and what it orders (3)

## Why this chapter

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the korrpon of a
glimnyr, there is at most one iskreld and no jenvex pairs exist.

D8. The korrpon of a glimnyr. The korrpon of a glimnyr x, written [x], is the smallest

Worked out for each glimnyr: duthquil to duthquil; ovivash to duthquil, ovivash, sibmi
and vintzel; sibmi to duthquil and sibmi; vintzel to duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and
vintzel.

Picture the korrpon as what happens when you start with one glimnyr and keep folding it

    ovivash @ duthquil = ovivash   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
    ovivash @ ovivash = sibmi   (the table for @)
So (ovivash @ duthquil) @ (sibmi @ vintzel) is sibmi.

A companion case, duthquil @ (sibmi @ ovivash), to show what the brackets are doing.
    sibmi @ ovivash = vintzel   (the table for @)
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
That gives vintzel, against sibmi above.

A second case, this time a korrpon. Start from duthquil. Combine it with itself, add

## Proofs

T14. No two distinct glimnyrs can both be iskrelds.

  (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors.
  (2) [D9] Then f >> h, since h is any object, and h >> f likewise.
  (3) [A7] Antisymmetry forces f = h.

Checked over 16 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T15. No two distinct glimnyrs lie in each other's opaltu.

  (1) [D14] Suppose x and y form a tight pair.
  (2) [A7] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y.
  (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise.

Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T7 rests on D8 (the korrpon of a glimnyr) and T6 (the korrpon of a glimnyr is rastsib).
Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being
provable.

T8 rests on D1 (rasttez glimnyrs), D12 (the nyrthra of a glimnyr) and T6 (the korrpon of
a glimnyr is rastsib). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not
merely stops being provable.

T9 rests on D12 (the nyrthra of a glimnyr) and T6 (the korrpon of a glimnyr is rastsib).
Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being
provable.

## A worked case

Take (vintzel @ ovivash) @ duthquil and work it out one step at a time.
    vintzel @ ovivash = duthquil   (the table for @)
    duthquil @ duthquil = duthquil   (the table for @)
The expression comes to duthquil.

Move the brackets and the work changes. Take ovivash @ (duthquil @ vintzel).
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
    ovivash @ vintzel = duthquil   (the table for @)
That gives duthquil, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does
duthquil >> sibmi hold? Read off what duthquil stands over: duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and
vintzel. sibmi is among them, so it holds.

## A case that breaks

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth
saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of glimnyrs that come back
unchanged from themselves: duthquil. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to
avoid.

## Reach and limits

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not.

The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation, association of the
first operation, closure under the first operation and reversal under the first
operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to
prove; it is a system where they are false.

To see how little the notation guarantees: rebuild the system with the same names over
different tables and T17 and T9 fail outright.

## Neighbouring results

The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (rasttez glimnyrs), D10 (zamyuk glimnyrs),
D11 (the dribra of a glimnyr) and D12 (the nyrthra of a glimnyr).

## Proofs

T10. If x lies in the tezfex then every glimnyr of [x] lies in the tezfex.

  (1) [T5] The tezfex is rastsib.
  (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest rastsib collection containing x.
  (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the tezfex is one.

Checked over 16 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T17. There is a glimnyr whose korrpon is the whole system.

  (1) [D8] Compute [x] for each glimnyr in turn.
  (2) [D12] The claim is that some nyrthra equals 4.
  (3) The search runs over finitely many objects, so it settles.

Checked over 4 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T4. If x @ x is the solglim then the dribra of x is x itself.

  (1) [D10] Let x be zamyuk, so x @ x is the solglim.
  (2) [D11] That is exactly the condition for x to be a partner of x.
  (3) [T3] Partners are unique, so no other object can be one.

Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T7. If S is rastsib and contains x, then S contains all of [x].

  (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation.
  (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications.
  (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications.

Checked over 12 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T8. x @ x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone.

  (1) [D1] If x @ x = x then {x} is already closed under @.
  (2) [T6] So [x] = {x} and the nyrthra is one.
  (3) [D12] Conversely a span of one object must contain x @ x, which is then x.

Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T9. For every glimnyr x, the nyrthra of x divides 4.

  (1) [T6] [x] is a rastsib collection.
  (2) [D12] Its size is the nyrthra of x.
  (3) The claim is that this size always divides 4.

Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: the mornrast. Each of these is used by name later, so
the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

Established here and safe to use: T10, T17, T4, T7, T8 and T9.

# Chapter 1. The objects and their notation

## Why this chapter

So far the glimnyrs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking
what they are like. We take up the Fextarn signature, the Fextarn combination tables and
closure under the first operation.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that
breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing
which do.

## The tables in full

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top.

          |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
---------------------------------------------------
 duthquil |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
  ovivash |   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel   vintzel
    sibmi |     sibmi   vintzel   vintzel   vintzel
  vintzel |   vintzel   vintzel   vintzel   vintzel

Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument.

  duthquil >> duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel
  ovivash >> vintzel
  sibmi >> vintzel
  vintzel >> vintzel

## What is defined here

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running
through the tables in full.

A1. Closure under the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y, x @ y is again a
glimnyr.

A2. Association of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @
z).

A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

## The shape of it

A useful mental split: some glimnyrs are inert under the operation and some are not.
duthquil and vintzel come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and duthquil,
ovivash, sibmi and vintzel commute with everything.

The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a
substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

## Where these results come from

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short
enough to hold in mind.

R2 rests on S2 (the Fextarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the
statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

R3 rests on S2 (the Fextarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the
statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

## A worked case

Here is (duthquil @ sibmi) @ vintzel, reduced without skipping anything.
    duthquil @ sibmi = sibmi   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
That leaves vintzel, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

A companion case, sibmi @ (vintzel @ duthquil), to show what the brackets are doing.
    vintzel @ duthquil = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
That gives vintzel, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

Test vintzel >> vintzel. The opaltu of vintzel is vintzel, and vintzel lies inside it,
so the relation holds.

## A case that breaks

R2. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x. It fails at x = ovivash,
value = sibmi. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

R3. It is not the case that: For all glimnyrs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then y = z. It
fails at x = ovivash, y = sibmi, z = vintzel. One case is enough, and this is the
earliest one.

## Reach and limits

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not.

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables
with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters
around them.

## Neighbouring results

What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an
absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A7
(transitivity of the relation).

## Proofs

R2. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = ovivash, value = sibmi, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

R3. It is not the case that: For all glimnyrs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then y = z.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = ovivash, y = sibmi, z = vintzel, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are
recorded above.

# Chapter 5. The relation and what it orders (2)

## Why this chapter

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet jenvex pairs, rastsib
collections and a iskreld early, whether or not they go looking.

Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 3, and a reader who
has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult.

A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every
case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4
glimnyrs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their
counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

## What is defined here

D13. Jenvex pairs. Two distinct glimnyrs x and y form a jenvex pair when x >> y and y >>
x both hold, that is, when each lies in the opaltu of the other.

In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward.

D3. Rastsib collections. A collection S of glimnyrs is rastsib when x @ y belongs to S
for every pair x, y drawn from S.

D9. A iskreld. A glimnyr f is a iskreld when f >> y holds for every glimnyr y, that is,
when the opaltu of f is the whole system.

In this system that picks out duthquil, which is 1 of the 4 glimnyrs.

## The shape of it

The right picture for korrpon is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one glimnyr
in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2 and 3
glimnyrs depending on where it started.

The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each glimnyr casts a opaltu over what it
refines, and the sizes of those shadows here are 1 and 4. Sizes repeat, so the objects
do not line up in single file.

The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a
substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

## Where these results come from

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short
enough to hold in mind.

R10 rests on D4 (the opaltu of a glimnyr). The dependence is on the content of those
results, not only on their vocabulary.

T9 rests on D4 (the opaltu of a glimnyr) and A7 (transitivity of the relation). The
dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

## A worked case

Take (vintzel @ sibmi) @ ovivash and work it out one step at a time.
    vintzel @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
    vintzel @ ovivash = vintzel   (the table for @)
That leaves vintzel, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is sibmi @ (ovivash @ vintzel) for contrast.
    ovivash @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
That gives vintzel, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

Test sibmi >> sibmi. The opaltu of sibmi is vintzel, and sibmi lies outside it, so the
relation fails.

## A case that breaks

R10. It is not the case that: If x >> y then y >> x. The case that settles it: x =
duthquil, y = ovivash. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will
be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation and
transitivity of the relation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in
general.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation), A7
(transitivity of the relation) and D4 (the opaltu of a glimnyr).

What is built on it later: D8 (the korrpon of a glimnyr), T3 (the tezfex is rastsib), T4
(the korrpon of a glimnyr is rastsib) and T8 (the bravex is rastsib).

## Proofs

R10. It is not the case that: If x >> y then y >> x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = duthquil, y = ovivash, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T9. If y lies in the opaltu of x, then the opaltu of y is contained in the opaltu of x.

  (1) [D4] Let y satisfy x >> y and let z satisfy y >> z.
  (2) [A7] Transitivity gives x >> z.
  (3) [D4] So every member of the opaltu of y is a member of that of x.

Checked over 64 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: jenvex pairs, rastsib collections and a iskreld. Each
of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

The results now available are T9, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by
argument from analogy.

Do not carry forward R10. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are
recorded above.

# Chapter 7. The relation and what it orders (3)

## Why this chapter

The present chapter develops the korrpon of a glimnyr, there is at most one iskreld and
no jenvex pairs exist.

Prerequisites are real here: chapters 3 and 5 supply the notions the statements below
are phrased in.

A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every
case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4
glimnyrs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

## What is defined here

D8. The korrpon of a glimnyr. The korrpon of a glimnyr x, written [x], is the smallest
rastsib collection that contains x.

Worked out for each glimnyr: duthquil to duthquil; ovivash to ovivash, sibmi and
vintzel; sibmi to sibmi and vintzel; vintzel to vintzel.

## The shape of it

The right picture for korrpon is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one glimnyr

The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each glimnyr casts a opaltu over what it

## Where these results come from

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading
before the statement.

T10 rests on D9 (a iskreld) and A6 (antisymmetry of the relation). Remove any one of
them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

T11 rests on D13 (jenvex pairs) and A6 (antisymmetry of the relation). Remove any one of
them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

## A worked case

Here is (vintzel @ sibmi) @ duthquil, reduced without skipping anything.
    vintzel @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
    vintzel @ duthquil = vintzel   (the table for @)
So (vintzel @ sibmi) @ duthquil is vintzel.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is sibmi @ (duthquil @ vintzel) for contrast.
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
The value is vintzel. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist
reading anything general into that.

One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does

vintzel. sibmi is among them, so it holds.

Now compute [duthquil]. Fold duthquil against itself, then fold whatever appeared
against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is duthquil,

## A case that breaks

## Reach and limits

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables

## Neighbouring results

Read alongside A6 (antisymmetry of the relation), D13 (jenvex pairs), D3 (rastsib
collections) and D9 (a iskreld).

These results are used again in D11 (the nyrthra of a glimnyr), T4 (the korrpon of a
glimnyr is rastsib), T5 (the korrpon is contained in every rastsib collection) and T7
(the korrpon of a tezfex glimnyr stays in the tezfex).

## Proofs

T10. No two distinct glimnyrs can both be iskrelds.

  (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors.
  (2) [D9] Then f >> h, since h is any object, and h >> f likewise.
  (3) [A6] Antisymmetry forces f = h.

Checked over 16 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T11. No two distinct glimnyrs lie in each other's opaltu.

  (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair.
  (2) [A6] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y.
  (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise.

Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: the korrpon of a glimnyr. Each of these is used by
name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

Established here and safe to use: T10 and T11.

# Chapter 9. Collections that close on themselves

## Why this chapter

The results collected here were not found in this order. The nyrthra of a glimnyr, the
korrpon of a glimnyr is rastsib and the korrpon of a tezfex glimnyr stays in the tezfex
came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible.

reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult.

## What is defined here

D11. The nyrthra of a glimnyr. The nyrthra of a glimnyr x is the number of glimnyrs in
its korrpon [x].

Worked out for each glimnyr: duthquil to 1; ovivash to 3; sibmi to 2; vintzel to 1.

## The shape of it

The right picture for korrpon is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one glimnyr

Two questions sort the glimnyrs quickly. Does combining a glimnyr with itself change it?

## Where these results come from

T4 rests on D8 (the korrpon of a glimnyr) and D3 (rastsib collections). Remove any one

T7 rests on D8 (the korrpon of a glimnyr), D6 (the tezfex) and T3 (the tezfex is
rastsib). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their
vocabulary.

## A worked case

Evaluate (ovivash @ vintzel) @ sibmi. Each line below is one lookup in a table.
    ovivash @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
    vintzel @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
So (ovivash @ vintzel) @ sibmi is vintzel.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is vintzel @ (sibmi @ ovivash) for contrast.
    sibmi @ ovivash = vintzel   (the table for @)
    vintzel @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
That gives vintzel, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does
sibmi >> duthquil hold? Read off what sibmi stands over: vintzel. duthquil is not among
them, so it fails.

against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is duthquil,

not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first
operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to
prove; it is a system where they are false.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

Read alongside D3 (rastsib collections), D6 (the tezfex), D8 (the korrpon of a glimnyr)
and T3 (the tezfex is rastsib).

What is built on it later: D12 (the mornrast), T5 (the korrpon is contained in every
rastsib collection), T6 (a glimnyr is rasttez exactly when its nyrthra is one) and R7
(where the nyrthra divides the number of glimnyrs breaks down).

## Proofs

T4. For every glimnyr x, the collection [x] is rastsib.

  (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under @.
  (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition.
  (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds.

Checked over 64 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T7. If x lies in the tezfex then every glimnyr of [x] lies in the tezfex.

  (1) [T3] The tezfex is rastsib.
  (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest rastsib collection containing x.
  (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the tezfex is one.

Checked over 16 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

Carry forward the nyrthra of a glimnyr. Later chapters state their results in these
terms and do not restate the definitions.

The results now available are T4 and T7, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by
argument from analogy.

# Chapter 10. Collections that close on themselves (2)

## Why this chapter

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet the mornrast, where the
nyrthra divides the number of glimnyrs breaks down and where some glimnyr reaches every
other breaks down early, whether or not they go looking.

Prerequisites are real here: chapters 4, 7 and 9 supply the notions the statements below
are phrased in.

counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

## What is defined here

D12. The mornrast. The mornrast of the system is the collection of glimnyrs whose
nyrthra is largest.

Running the definition over every glimnyr leaves ovivash.

## The shape of it

Picture the korrpon as what happens when you start with one glimnyr and keep folding it
against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there
are only 4 glimnyrs, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 3.

None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the
shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every
proof goes through the tables.

## Where these results come from

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short

[ch0] # Chapter 1. The objects and their notation

## Why this chapter

So far the glimnyrs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking
what they are like. We take up the Fextarn signature, the Fextarn combination tables and
closure under the first operation.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that
breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing
which do.

## The tables in full

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top.

          |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
---------------------------------------------------

  ovivash |   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil
    sibmi |     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash
  vintzel |   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi

Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument.

  duthquil >> duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel
  ovivash >> nothing
  sibmi >> nothing
  vintzel >> nothing

## What is defined here

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running
through the tables in full.

A1. Closure under the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y, x @ y is again a
glimnyr.

A2. Association of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @
z).

A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

A6. Cancellation in the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then
y = z.

## The shape of it

A useful mental split: some glimnyrs are inert under the operation and some are not.
duthquil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and duthquil, ovivash, sibmi
and vintzel commute with everything.

substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

enough to hold in mind.

So far the glimnyrs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking
what they are like. We take up the Fextarn signature, the Fextarn combination tables and
closure under the first operation.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that
breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing
which do.

## The tables in full

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top.

          |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
---------------------------------------------------
 duthquil |  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel
  ovivash |   ovivash     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil
    sibmi |     sibmi   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash
  vintzel |   vintzel  duthquil   ovivash     sibmi

Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument.

  duthquil >> duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel
  ovivash >> nothing
  sibmi >> nothing
  vintzel >> nothing

## What is defined here

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running
through the tables in full.

A1. Closure under the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y, x @ y is again a
glimnyr.

A2. Association of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @
z).

A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all glimnyrs x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

A6. Cancellation in the first operation. For all glimnyrs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then
y = z.

## The shape of it

A useful mental split: some glimnyrs are inert under the operation and some are not.
duthquil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and duthquil, ovivash, sibmi
and vintzel commute with everything.

The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a
substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a
system with 4 glimnyrs the table is short enough to consult every time.

## Where these results come from

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short
enough to hold in mind.

R1 rests on S2 (the Fextarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the
statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

## A worked case

Here is (duthquil @ sibmi) @ vintzel, reduced without skipping anything.
    duthquil @ sibmi = sibmi   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
That leaves ovivash, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

A companion case, sibmi @ (vintzel @ duthquil), to show what the brackets are doing.
    vintzel @ duthquil = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = ovivash   (the table for @)
That gives ovivash, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these
particular arguments and not a law.

Test vintzel >> vintzel. The opaltu of vintzel is empty, and vintzel lies outside it, so
the relation fails.

## A case that breaks

R1. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x. The case that settles it: x
= ovivash, value = sibmi. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system
will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (reversal
under the first operation), A7 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A8 (transitivity of
the relation).

## Proofs

R1. It is not the case that: For every glimnyr x: x @ x = x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case x = ovivash, value = sibmi, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is
wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.


[ch1] # Chapter 2. Neutral objects and reversal

## Why this chapter

We turn to a neutral object for the first operation, reversal under the first operation
and the system does not have an absorbing object for the first operation. The treatment
is self contained given the material already established.

Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are
phrased in.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their
counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

## What is defined here

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was
written down.

A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a glimnyr duthquil with duthquil
@ x = x @ duthquil = x for every x.

A5. Reversal under the first operation. For every glimnyr x there is a glimnyr y with x
@ y = y @ x = duthquil.

## The shape of it

The neutral glimnyr duthquil is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is
not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces.

None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the
shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every
proof goes through the tables.

## Where these results come from

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading
before the statement.

R2 rests on S2 (the Fextarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the
statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

## A worked case

Here is (sibmi @ duthquil) @ (ovivash @ vintzel), reduced without skipping anything.
    sibmi @ duthquil = sibmi   (the table for @)
    ovivash @ vintzel = duthquil   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ duthquil = sibmi   (the table for @)
The expression comes to sibmi.

A companion case, duthquil @ (ovivash @ sibmi), to show what the brackets are doing.
    ovivash @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
The value is vintzel, not sibmi.

One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does
sibmi >> ovivash hold? Read off what sibmi stands over: nothing at all. ovivash is not
among them, so it fails.

## A case that breaks

R2. There is no glimnyr z with z @ x = x @ z = z for every glimnyr x. The case that
settles it: reason = no absorbing element. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more
familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

## Reach and limits

The limits of these results are sharper than they look.

Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours.
Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

## Neighbouring results

The material this chapter borrows from: S2 (the Fextarn combination tables).

These results are used again in D5 (the solglim), D11 (the dribra of a glimnyr) and T1
(the solglim is the only one of its kind).

## Proofs

R2. There is no glimnyr z with z @ x = x @ z = z for every glimnyr x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case reason = no absorbing element, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

Explicitly not available: R2. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is
wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.


[ch3] # Chapter 4. Combining objects

## Why this chapter

The results collected here were not found in this order. Rasttez glimnyrs, glimnyrs that
falhurn and the solglim came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the
pattern was visible.

Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who
has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult.

The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimnyrs covers at
most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an
argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

## What is defined here

D1. Rasttez glimnyrs. A glimnyr x is called rasttez when x @ x = x.

Running the definition over every glimnyr leaves duthquil.

D2. Glimnyrs that falhurn. Two glimnyrs x and y are said to falhurn when x @ y = y @ x.

D5. The solglim. The glimnyr duthquil is called the solglim of the system. It is the
unique glimnyr that leaves every glimnyr unchanged under @.

Here that is duthquil.

## The shape of it

Two questions sort the glimnyrs quickly. Does combining a glimnyr with itself change it?
For duthquil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For duthquil, ovivash,
sibmi and vintzel it does not.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single glimnyr and,
through that, constrains everything that can combine with it.

None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the
shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every
proof goes through the tables.

## Where these results come from

This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

## A worked case

Take (sibmi @ duthquil) @ (ovivash @ vintzel) and work it out one step at a time.
    sibmi @ duthquil = sibmi   (the table for @)
    ovivash @ vintzel = duthquil   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ duthquil = sibmi   (the table for @)
That leaves sibmi, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is duthquil @ (ovivash @ sibmi) for contrast.
    ovivash @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
The value is vintzel, not sibmi.

Test ovivash >> ovivash. The opaltu of ovivash is empty, and ovivash lies outside it, so
the relation fails.

## A case that breaks

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth
saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of glimnyrs that come back
unchanged from themselves: duthquil. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to
avoid.

## Reach and limits

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not.

The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the
first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to
prove; it is a system where they are false.

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables
with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters
around them.

## Neighbouring results

Read alongside A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the
first operation).

These results are used again in D6 (the tezfex), D7 (the bravex), D10 (zamyuk glimnyrs)
and D11 (the dribra of a glimnyr).

## Proofs

No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: rasttez glimnyrs, glimnyrs that falhurn and the
solglim. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather
than looking up.

D5. The solglim. The glimnyr duthquil is called the solglim of the system. It is the
unique glimnyr that leaves every glimnyr unchanged under @.

Two questions sort the glimnyrs quickly. Does combining a glimnyr with itself change it?
For duthquil and vintzel it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For
duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel it does not.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single glimnyr and,
through that, constrains everything that can combine with it.

None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the
shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every
proof goes through the tables.

## Where these results come from

This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

## A worked case

Take (sibmi @ duthquil) @ (ovivash @ vintzel) and work it out one step at a time.

    ovivash @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
That leaves vintzel, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is duthquil @ (ovivash @ sibmi) for contrast.
    ovivash @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
The value is vintzel. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist
reading anything general into that.

Test ovivash >> ovivash. The opaltu of ovivash is vintzel, and ovivash lies outside it,
so the relation fails.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth
saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of glimnyrs that come back
unchanged from themselves: duthquil and vintzel. Assuming more of them than that is the
mistake to avoid.

## Reach and limits

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not.

The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the
first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to
prove; it is a system where they are false.

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables
with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters
around them.

## Neighbouring results

Read alongside A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the
first operation).

These results are used again in D6 (the tezfex), D7 (the bravex), D10 (zamyuk glimnyrs)
and T1 (the solglim is the only one of its kind).

## Proofs

No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.

solglim. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather

## Why this chapter

So far the glimnyrs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking
what they are like. We take up zamyuk glimnyrs, the tezfex and the bravex.

Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 2 and 4, and a reader who
has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult.

A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every
case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4
glimnyrs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that
breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing
which do.

## What is defined here

D10. Zamyuk glimnyrs. A glimnyr x is zamyuk when x @ x equals the solglim.

Running the definition over every glimnyr leaves duthquil.

D6. The tezfex. The tezfex of the system is the collection of glimnyrs that falhurn with
every glimnyr.

Running the definition over every glimnyr leaves duthquil, ovivash, sibmi and vintzel.

D7. The bravex. The bravex is the collection of all rasttez glimnyrs.

Running the definition over every glimnyr leaves duthquil and vintzel.

## The shape of it

A useful mental split: some glimnyrs are inert under the operation and some are not.
duthquil and vintzel come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and duthquil,
ovivash, sibmi and vintzel commute with everything.

The neutral glimnyr duthquil is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is
not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces.

None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the
shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every
proof goes through the tables.

## Where these results come from

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading
before the statement.

R11 rests on D5 (the solglim). The dependence is on the content of those results, not
only on their vocabulary.

T1 rests on D5 (the solglim) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). The
dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

## A worked case

Here is (duthquil @ vintzel) @ (sibmi @ ovivash), reduced without skipping anything.
    duthquil @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
    sibmi @ ovivash = vintzel   (the table for @)
    vintzel @ vintzel = vintzel   (the table for @)
The expression comes to vintzel.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is vintzel @ (sibmi @ duthquil) for contrast.
    sibmi @ duthquil = sibmi   (the table for @)
    vintzel @ sibmi = vintzel   (the table for @)
The value is vintzel. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist
reading anything general into that.

One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does
duthquil >> ovivash hold? Read off what duthquil stands over: duthquil, ovivash, sibmi
and vintzel. ovivash is among them, so it holds.

## A case that breaks

R11. It is not the case that: e @ x equals the solglim for every glimnyr x. It fails at
anchor = duthquil, x = ovivash, value = ovivash. One case is enough, and this is the
earliest one.

## Reach and limits

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not.

Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation
and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of
systems in general.

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables
with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters
around them.

## Neighbouring results

Read alongside A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (rasttez glimnyrs), D2
(glimnyrs that falhurn) and D5 (the solglim).

What is built on it later: T2 (the solglim lies in the tezfex), T3 (the tezfex is
rastsib), T7 (the korrpon of a tezfex glimnyr stays in the tezfex) and T8 (the bravex is
rastsib).

## Proofs

R11. It is not the case that: e @ x equals the solglim for every glimnyr x.

  (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = duthquil, x = ovivash, value = ovivash, read straight from the tables.
  (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case.
  (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading.

Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T1. There is exactly one glimnyr e with e @ x = x @ e = x for every glimnyr x.

  (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every glimnyr unchanged.
  (2) [A4] Then e @ f = f, reading e as neutral on the left.
  (3) [A4] And e @ f = e, reading f as neutral on the right.
  (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object.

Checked over 16 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

## What to carry forward

New vocabulary from this chapter: zamyuk glimnyrs, the tezfex and the bravex. Each of
these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

Established here and safe to use: T1.

Do not carry forward R11. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are
recorded above.

The Solovi System.

The Solovi system introduces a single operator written ?. It combines two whole numbers and produces a whole number.

To evaluate x ? y, multiply x by 3, multiply y by 7, add the two products, then add 5.

Reduction in the Solovi system.

Every result in this system is reduced modulo 1000. That is, after computing a value you divide it by 1000 and keep only the remainder. A result is therefore always between 0 and 999 inclusive.

Evaluation order in the Solovi system.

When an expression contains more than one ?, the operator associates right to left. Parentheses, where written, are evaluated first.

A worked example.

Consider 7 ? 4. Applying the rule gives 54.
